title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework

hero.subtitle: The authorization framework that powers "Sign in with Google/GitHub/Facebook" and API access delegation across the modern web.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that enables third-party applications to obtain limited access to an HTTP service on behalf of a resource owner. Rather than sharing credentials, users delegate access through access tokens.

OAuth 2.0 is about authorization (what you can access), not authentication (who you are). OpenID Connect builds authentication on top of OAuth 2.0.
sections.eli5: Normally, to let an app use your photos you would hand it your password, and then it could do anything. OAuth lets you hand over a limited pass instead, so the app only gets what you agreed to.

sections.title: Roles
sections.content:
OAuth 2.0 defines four roles:

Resource OwnerThe user who authorizes access to their account
ClientThe application requesting access on behalf of the user
Authorization ServerIssues access tokens after authenticating the resource owner
Resource ServerHosts the protected resources, validates access tokens
sections.eli5: There are four characters: you, the app that wants help, the office that hands out passes, and the place that keeps your stuff and checks the passes.

sections.title: Grant Types
sections.content:
OAuth 2.0 defines several flows for obtaining access tokens, each suited to different application types:

Grant Type
Use Case
Authorization Code
Web apps with a backend server (most secure)
Implicit
Browser-based SPAs (deprecated in favor of Auth Code + PKCE)
Resource Owner Password
Trusted first-party apps only (discouraged)
Client Credentials
Machine-to-machine API access

The Implicit grant type is now considered insecure. Use Authorization Code with PKCE (RFC 7636) for all public clients including SPAs and mobile apps.
sections.eli5: There is more than one way to get a pass, depending on what kind of app is asking. Some ways are safer than others, and the old risky ones are being retired.

sections.title: Access Tokens & Refresh Tokens
sections.content:
Access tokens are credentials used to access protected resources. They have a limited lifetime and specific scope.

Access Token
Short-lived credential (minutes to hours) sent with API requests via Authorization header
Refresh Token
Long-lived credential used to obtain new access tokens without user interaction
Scope
Limits what resources the token can access (e.g., "read:email write:profile")
Using a Bearer Token
GET /api/user/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...
sections.eli5: The pass works for a short time and says what it opens. If it runs out, a longer-lasting ticket can get a new one without bothering you again.

subtitle: The authorization framework that powers "Sign in with Google/GitHub/Facebook" and API access delegation across the modern web.

eli5.summary: Instead of giving an app your password, you give it a special pass that opens only the doors you chose, and you can take the pass back whenever you like.

questions: what is the difference between authentication and authorization
how does the authorization code flow work
why is the implicit grant discouraged

tldr.problem: Giving a third-party app your password lets it do everything and cannot be taken back without changing the password.
tldr.mechanism: The user approves the app at an authorization server, which issues the app a limited, expiring access token to present to the resource server.
tldr.outcome: Apps get narrow, revocable access without ever seeing the user's password; it became the basis of "Sign in with" and API access across the web.

facts.label: Grant types
facts.value: 4 (code, implicit, password, client credentials), plus extension grants

today: OAuth 2.0 is everywhere: social login buttons, mobile apps calling APIs, and service-to-service access all use it. In practice most deployments follow later guidance, using the authorization code grant with PKCE (RFC 7636) and avoiding the implicit and password grants. OpenID Connect adds a sign-in layer on top.
